# Tools and alternatives

Every tool Penlark names, scored by the shared method (`COMPARISON-METHOD.md` in the hub): six weighted criteria (fit 35, setup effort 15, reliability and upkeep 15, cost 15, data control 10, integration depth 10), each 0 to 100 with a written evidence line. Closeness is the alternative's fit divided by the reference tool's fit. These are judgements from sources and our own adapter work, not benchmarks. No prices are quoted.

<!-- SCORES:START (generated by tools/score_tools.py, do not edit by hand) -->

Scores dated 2026-11-23. Judgements from sources and our own adapter work on the date shown, not benchmarks. A tool marked not run was never used against the real vendor.

### Where an approved post goes to be scheduled or published

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Buffer | paid | 75 | 80 | 80 | 60 | 45 | 70 | **70.8** | reference |
| Metricool | paid | 78 | 70 | 75 | 60 | 45 | 50 | **67.5** | 104 percent of Buffer |
| Postiz | open source | 72 | 50 | 60 | 85 | 90 | 80 | **71.5** | 96 percent of Buffer |
| File export | built in | 50 | 100 | 95 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **81.8** | 67 percent of Buffer |

What Penlark has for each: Buffer: Adapter written from the developer docs, saves a draft by default (not run against Buffer); Metricool: Adapter written from memory, UNVERIFIED (not run against Metricool); Postiz: Adapter written from the public API docs, tested against a local stand in (not run against Postiz); File export: Built in, the default (run and tested).

**Evidence, Buffer**

- Fit (75): A familiar queue and calendar that many creators already use, with a GraphQL API for drafts.
- Setup effort (80): Create a token in the Buffer settings and paste it in. No server to run.
- Reliability and upkeep (80): A hosted service with a clear status page. Network approvals are Buffer's job, not yours.
- Cost (60): Paid plans for several channels. See the vendor price page, no figure is quoted here.
- Data control (45): Posts and tokens sit with the vendor. You cannot run it on your own server.
- Integration depth (70): Penlark calls the createPost mutation and defaults to saveToDraft, so a person still presses publish.
- Sources: https://developers.buffer.com/examples/create-draft-post.html (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Metricool**

- Fit (78): Scheduling plus built in analytics and reports in one tool, which suits a performance review loop.
- Setup effort (70): Needs a token, a user id and a blog id. The steps could not be read from the docs.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): A hosted service with a long track record. API access may depend on the plan.
- Cost (60): Paid plans. API access may need a higher one. Check the vendor page.
- Data control (45): Data sits with the vendor.
- Integration depth (50): The request shape is from memory, so the adapter is the least certain of the three.
- Sources: https://metricool.com/api/ (checked page did not describe the API)

**Evidence, Postiz**

- Fit (72): Schedules to many networks from one open source tool and has a public API with drafts and scheduling.
- Setup effort (50): Self hosting needs Docker, a database and each network's app keys. Cloud is easier.
- Reliability and upkeep (60): You carry updates and uptime. The docs list a default limit of 90 create requests an hour.
- Cost (85): Free to self host. Pay only for a small server. A cloud plan exists with its own price page.
- Data control (90): Posts and keys stay on your server when self hosted.
- Integration depth (80): The adapter sends the documented body: type, date, posts with integration id and content, settings type.
- Sources: https://docs.postiz.com/public-api/introduction (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, File export**

- Fit (50): No scheduling and no reach: it only saves the text so a person posts it by hand.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to install or set up at all.
- Reliability and upkeep (95): A local file cannot go down or be rate limited.
- Cost (100): It costs nothing to use.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves your machine.
- Integration depth (100): It is the one path that works with no account and cannot publish.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/penlark (checked this repo)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Start with the file export: Penlark saves the approved text and you paste it into LinkedIn or X yourself. It needs no account and nothing can be sent by mistake. Add a scheduler later.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Buffer and Postiz were read from their docs and tested only against local stand ins. Metricool is from memory. Pick the one your client already pays for, keep the mode in draft, and test with one real account first.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** The file export costs nothing. Postiz is open source and costs a small server. Buffer and Metricool have price pages: read them yourself, none is quoted here.
- **When open source is the right call:** Postiz is the right call when the client wants posts to stay on their own server and someone can run Docker. It is the wrong call when the client wants someone else to handle each network's app approval and outages.

### Short links that show which post brought a click

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bitly | paid | 70 | 85 | 85 | 55 | 40 | 30 | **65.2** | reference |
| Dub | open source | 72 | 50 | 60 | 80 | 90 | 30 | **65.7** | 103 percent of Bitly |
| Penlark tracked links | built in | 60 | 95 | 75 | 100 | 95 | 100 | **81.0** | 86 percent of Bitly |

What Penlark has for each: Bitly: Not built, any shortener's address can go in a post by hand (not run); Dub: Not built, named as an alternative (not run); Penlark tracked links: Built in, tested (run and tested).

**Evidence, Bitly**

- Fit (70): Very well known short links with a dashboard and a branded domain option.
- Setup effort (85): Sign up and paste a link. Nothing to host.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): A hosted service with a long record.
- Cost (55): Paid plans for branded domains and more links. See the vendor page.
- Data control (40): Click data sits with the vendor.
- Integration depth (30): Penlark has no Bitly adapter. You would paste links by hand and import clicks later.
- Sources: https://bitly.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Dub**

- Fit (72): Open source link management with analytics and custom domains, from its own site.
- Setup effort (50): Self hosting needs a database and several services. A hosted plan exists.
- Reliability and upkeep (60): You carry updates when self hosted.
- Cost (80): Self hosting costs a server. A hosted plan has its own price page.
- Data control (90): Click data stays with you when self hosted.
- Integration depth (30): Penlark has no Dub adapter. Links would be pasted by hand and clicks imported as CSV.
- Sources: https://dub.co/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Penlark tracked links**

- Fit (60): Short links with UTM tags, a click count, unique visitors and lead conversions next to each post. No branded dashboard.
- Setup effort (95): Needs only a public address for the app and an allow list of your own hosts.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): One public route, rate limited, with an allow list checked again on every click.
- Cost (100): It costs nothing to use.
- Data control (95): Clicks are stored with a one day hash, never an address.
- Integration depth (100): It is the tracker the funnel page reads, so no import is needed.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/penlark (checked this repo)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the built in tracked links. They add the UTM tags for you and show clicks and leads next to each post. You only need your own website address on the allow list.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Keep the built in links for posts and keep the allow list short. If the client already has Bitly or Dub, keep using it and import the clicks as a CSV later. Point the short domain at the app.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** The built in links cost nothing. Dub can be self hosted. Bitly has a price page: read it yourself, no figure is quoted here.
- **When open source is the right call:** Self hosted Dub is the right call when you need a branded short domain with a full dashboard and can run a database. For one person with one site, the built in links are enough.

### What writes the first draft

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anthropic model | paid | 90 | 70 | 85 | 55 | 40 | 45 | **71.5** | reference |
| Offline templates | built in | 40 | 100 | 95 | 100 | 100 | 100 | **78.2** | 44 percent of Anthropic model |

What Penlark has for each: Anthropic model: Real code through the shared wrapper, fake server only, UNVERIFIED (never run live); Offline templates: Built in, tested (run and tested).

**Evidence, Anthropic model**

- Fit (90): Writes real sentences in a voice from a guide and evidence, which templates cannot.
- Setup effort (70): Needs an API key and a spend limit set by the owner.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): A hosted service, with retries in the shared wrapper.
- Cost (55): Billed per use. See the vendor page.
- Data control (40): Prompts leave your machine. Sample text is passed as untrusted data.
- Integration depth (45): The code path exists and is tested against a fake server only. Output goes through every check.
- Sources: https://docs.anthropic.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Offline templates**

- Fit (40): Fills a template from your evidence and voice numbers. It is not a language model and it leaves brackets where facts are needed.
- Setup effort (100): Nothing to install or set up at all.
- Reliability and upkeep (95): Deterministic, the same input gives the same output.
- Cost (100): It costs nothing to use.
- Data control (100): Nothing leaves your machine.
- Integration depth (100): It is the default writer and the one the demo uses.
- Sources: https://github.com/onittindwani-ai/penlark (checked this repo)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Leave it on the offline templates. They give a skeleton in your style with brackets for every real fact, so nothing is invented. You write the facts.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Wire the live model only after you have read the held out match numbers. The live path was never run with a real key. It must still pass the voice match, house rules and claims check before a person sees an approve button.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Offline templates cost nothing. A live model is billed per use. See the vendor price page, no figure is quoted here.
- **When open source is the right call:** No open source model is built in. If a client needs text to stay on their own machine, ask Claude Code to write an adapter for a local model, and run the held out voice test on its output first.

### Where the app runs

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vercel | paid | 80 | 90 | 85 | 65 | 50 | 60 | **75.0** | reference |
| Railway | paid | 80 | 75 | 75 | 60 | 50 | 70 | **71.5** | 100 percent of Vercel |
| Hetzner server | paid | 85 | 45 | 60 | 90 | 95 | 80 | **76.5** | 106 percent of Vercel |

What Penlark has for each: Vercel: Guide written, web part only (not run on Vercel); Railway: Config file written, not run (not run on Railway); Hetzner server: Compose, Caddy, backup and cloud init files written, not run (not run on Hetzner).

**Evidence, Vercel**

- Fit (80): Built for Next.js: import the repo, set the root directory to apps/web, set two variables.
- Setup effort (90): Few steps and preview deployments.
- Reliability and upkeep (85): Managed. Cannot run the API or worker, which need a long running process.
- Cost (65): A free tier exists and paid plans follow. See the vendor page.
- Data control (50): Hosted with the vendor.
- Integration depth (60): Only the web app goes here. The API lives elsewhere.
- Sources: https://vercel.com/docs/monorepos (checked 2026-11-23)

**Evidence, Railway**

- Fit (80): Runs the API and worker as two services with a Postgres add on from one repo.
- Setup effort (75): Connect the repo, set variables, add Postgres.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Managed, with health checks and logs.
- Cost (60): Usage based. See the vendor page.
- Data control (50): Hosted with the vendor.
- Integration depth (70): A railway.json is in the repo. Its format was not re checked against the current docs.
- Sources: https://docs.railway.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, Hetzner server**

- Fit (85): One small server runs everything with Docker Compose and automatic HTTPS.
- Setup effort (45): You set up the server, firewall, updates and backups yourself, with the guide.
- Reliability and upkeep (60): You carry upkeep and updates.
- Cost (90): Usually the cheapest of the three. See the vendor page.
- Data control (95): Everything stays on a server you control.
- Integration depth (80): A compose file, a Caddyfile, a backup script and a cloud init file are in the repo.
- Sources: https://docs.hetzner.com/ (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Run it on your own computer first with the demo. For a first real use, Vercel for the web part and Railway for the rest is the easiest path in these guides.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Vercel plus Railway for a quick client start, or everything on one Hetzner server when the client wants one bill and full control. Use a tunnel for webhook testing at home.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** A single small Hetzner server is usually the cheapest way to run the API and database. Vercel has a free tier for hobby use. Read each price page yourself.
- **When open source is the right call:** Not a question of open source here: all three run the same open code. Pick by who does the upkeep.

### Where the data is kept

| Tool | Kind | Fit (35) | Setup effort (15) | Reliability and upkeep (15) | Cost (15) | Data control (10) | Integration depth (10) | Total | Closeness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | open source | 90 | 60 | 90 | 80 | 95 | 85 | **84.0** | reference |
| SQLite | open source | 65 | 100 | 75 | 100 | 100 | 95 | **83.5** | 72 percent of PostgreSQL |

What Penlark has for each: PostgreSQL: Supported through the same models and migration (migration cycle run on a throwaway Postgres 17); SQLite: Supported, the default for the demo (full suites run on SQLite).

**Evidence, PostgreSQL**

- Fit (90): Handles the web app and the worker at the same time and is what the deploy files use.
- Setup effort (60): A service to run, or a managed add on.
- Reliability and upkeep (90): Very reliable with backups.
- Cost (80): Free software. Server or plan cost only.
- Data control (95): You control the data.
- Integration depth (85): Same models. The full suites were not run on it.
- Sources: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/ (checked not fetched)

**Evidence, SQLite**

- Fit (65): Fine for one person and a demo. One writer at a time, so the worker and web app can briefly wait on each other.
- Setup effort (100): A file, nothing to install.
- Reliability and upkeep (75): Reliable for small loads. Copy the file to back it up.
- Cost (100): It costs nothing to use.
- Data control (100): A file on your machine.
- Integration depth (95): Same models, WAL mode on.
- Sources: https://www.sqlite.org/docs.html (checked not fetched)

**Recommendation by user type**

- **Beginner:** Use the built in SQLite file for the demo and for one person on one computer. Nothing to install.
- **Implementer running it for clients:** Use Postgres for any real deployment. The migration was run up, down and up on Postgres 17, but the full test and browser suites ran on SQLite only.
- **Cost sensitive owner:** Both are free software. Postgres costs a small server or a managed plan.
- **When open source is the right call:** Both are open source. Choose SQLite for a single user on one machine, Postgres when the web app and worker run as separate services.

### Named but not scored

- LinkedIn, X, Instagram, Facebook and other network APIs: Each network requires its own app approval. The scheduler tool you choose holds that approval, so Penlark does not call these networks directly.
- Cloudflare Tunnel and Cloudflare DNS: Named in the deploy guides for webhook testing and a custom domain. They are infrastructure, not a choice Penlark depends on.
- A form or CRM tool that sends lead events: Any tool that can send a signed webhook works. None is built in, so none is scored.
